title: Best Hangover Breakfast: 5 Easy Recipes That Actually Help
excerpt: The best breakfast for a hangover, with five easy recipes, what to eat when you feel sick, whether greasy food helps, and what to drink with it.
metaDescription: The best hangover breakfast: 5 easy recipes, what to eat if you feel sick, whether greasy food helps, fast food picks, and what to drink with it.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best hangover breakfast is a gentle, balanced plate: some protein (eggs or yogurt), easy carbohydrates (toast, oats, rice, or a banana), a little salt, and plenty of fluid. That combination steadies your energy, settles your stomach, and helps replace some of the water and salts alcohol pushed out of your body. No breakfast cures a hangover. There is no good evidence that any single food shortens one. But eating the right thing at the right time makes the morning much easier, and eating the wrong thing (a huge greasy fry-up washed down with more coffee than water) can make it worse.

**The quick plan for this morning:** drink a big glass of water or an electrolyte drink first. If your stomach is shaky, start with dry toast or a banana and wait 30 to 60 minutes. Once that stays down, have one of the five breakfasts below. Soft scrambled eggs on toast is the safest bet for most people.

> **When to see a doctor.** A normal hangover is unpleasant but fades within a day. Get medical help if you or someone else **can't keep fluids down for several hours**, **keeps vomiting**, **vomits blood or something that looks like coffee grounds**, has **severe stomach pain**, is **confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake**, has **a seizure**, or has **slow or irregular breathing**. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning or serious dehydration, not a hangover. If you get **shaky, sweaty, anxious, or see or hear things** a day or two after stopping drinking, especially after several days of heavy drinking in a row, that can be alcohol withdrawal and needs medical care. In an emergency, call 911.

## Why Breakfast Helps When You're Hungover

A hangover is not one thing. It's a bundle of effects that hit at the same time, and food helps with some of them but not others. Knowing which is which explains why certain breakfasts work better than others.

**What food can help with:**

- **Low energy and shakiness.** Alcohol interferes with how your liver releases stored sugar into your blood, and many people skip dinner or eat badly on a night out. Researchers still debate how much low blood sugar drives hangover symptoms, but most people feel steadier and less weak once they've eaten. Carbohydrates are the fastest way to get there.
- **Mild dehydration and lost salts.** Alcohol makes you urinate more than you drink, and you lose sodium and potassium along the way. Water, salty foods, and potassium-rich foods like bananas help put some of that back.
- **An irritated stomach.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining and increases acid. Bland, soft foods are easier to tolerate than spicy, acidic, or very greasy ones.
- **Making medicine gentler.** If you need a painkiller, taking it with food is kinder to your stomach. (See the note on painkillers further down.)

**What food can't fix:**

- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol fragments the second half of the night, so you wake up tired no matter what you eat.
- **Inflammation and the immune response.** A big part of how rough you feel comes from your body's inflammatory reaction to alcohol. Breakfast doesn't switch that off.
- **Acetaldehyde.** This toxic by-product of alcohol is cleared by your liver on its own schedule. Some foods contain nutrients involved in that process (more on eggs below), but you can't eat your way to a faster clearance in any meaningful amount.

So the goal of a hangover breakfast is simple: **rehydrate, refuel, and don't upset your stomach.** Everything below is built around that.

## What Makes a Good Hangover Breakfast

Before the recipes, here are the building blocks, so you can improvise with whatever is in your kitchen.

### 1. Easy carbohydrates

Toast, oats, rice, potatoes, bananas, and crackers are gentle and quick to digest. They're the base of every breakfast below. White toast or plain rice is easier on a queasy stomach; oats and whole-grain bread release energy more slowly and keep you full longer once you're feeling steadier.

### 2. Gentle protein

Eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, tofu, or a little chicken. Protein makes the meal last longer, so you don't crash an hour later. Eggs are the classic choice for a reason: they're soft, mild, cheap, and contain cysteine, an amino acid your body uses to make glutathione, one of the liver's main antioxidants. That's real chemistry, but the amount in a couple of eggs is modest. Our guide to [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover) goes through the science in detail.

### 3. Salt and potassium

A pinch of salt on your eggs, a bowl of broth, a banana, a potato, avocado, or a glass of coconut water. These help replace the minerals alcohol flushed out. You don't need to overthink this. A normal, lightly salted breakfast plus a banana covers most of it.

### 4. Fluid, and lots of it

Start with a large glass of water before you eat anything, then keep sipping. If you drank heavily or were sick, an oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix is a better bet than plain water because it contains salt and a little sugar, which help your body absorb the fluid. Our guide on [whether to take electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers timing and options.

### 5. Something mild for nausea

Ginger has decent evidence for easing nausea in other settings, such as pregnancy-related morning sickness, and many people find a cup of ginger tea settling the morning after. It has not been well tested specifically for hangovers. See our article on [ginger for a hangover](/never-hungover/ginger-for-hangover) for what's known.

## The 5 Best Hangover Breakfasts (With Recipes)

These are ordered roughly from "most people's first choice" to "for when your stomach is really unhappy." Each one takes 15 minutes or less.

### 1. Soft Scrambled Eggs on Toast with Avocado

**Best for:** most hangovers. It's the all-rounder.

**Why it works:** eggs give you gentle protein and some cysteine, toast gives you easy carbs, and avocado adds potassium and a little healthy fat without the heaviness of fried food. Soft scrambled eggs are much easier on a queasy stomach than crispy fried ones.

**Ingredients (serves 1):**

- 2 eggs
- 1 tablespoon milk (optional)
- 1 small knob of butter or a teaspoon of olive oil
- 1 or 2 slices of bread (sourdough or whole grain if your stomach is fine, plain white if it isn't)
- Half a ripe avocado
- Salt and pepper
- Optional: a handful of spinach, chopped chives, a few cherry tomatoes

**How to make it:**

1. Put a glass of water next to the stove and drink it while you cook.
2. Crack the eggs into a bowl, add the milk and a pinch of salt, and whisk with a fork.
3. Melt the butter in a nonstick pan over **low** heat. Low heat is the secret to soft, creamy eggs.
4. Pour in the eggs and stir slowly with a spatula, pushing them from the edges to the middle. If using spinach, add it now so it wilts.
5. Take the pan off the heat when the eggs are just set but still look slightly wet. They'll finish cooking on the plate.
6. Toast the bread, mash the avocado on top with a pinch of salt, and pile the eggs over it.

**Make it easier:** if your stomach is unsettled, skip the avocado and pepper and just have eggs on plain toast. Add the extras next time.

### 2. Banana, Oat, and Ginger Smoothie

**Best for:** when you can't face chewing, or you need breakfast in a glass.

**Why it works:** a smoothie gets carbs, protein, potassium, and fluid into you at once, and it's easy to sip slowly. Banana and oats give you steady energy, yogurt adds protein, and fresh ginger may help with nausea. Using coconut water or milk as the base adds fluid and some potassium.

**Ingredients (serves 1):**

- 1 ripe banana (frozen makes it colder and thicker)
- 3 tablespoons rolled oats
- 150 g (about two-thirds of a cup) plain Greek yogurt
- 200 ml (about three-quarters of a cup) coconut water, milk, or water
- A thumb-sized piece of fresh ginger, peeled, or a quarter teaspoon of ground ginger
- 1 teaspoon honey (optional)
- A small pinch of salt
- A few ice cubes

**How to make it:**

1. Put everything in a blender, oats first so they break down properly.
2. Blend for 45 to 60 seconds until smooth.
3. Taste. Add more honey if it's too tart, or more liquid if it's too thick.
4. Sip it slowly over 10 to 15 minutes rather than gulping it.

**Notes:** the pinch of salt sounds odd but you won't taste it, and it helps with rehydration. If dairy bothers you, swap the yogurt for a dairy-free yogurt or a spoonful of nut butter. Skip the ginger if you don't like the bite. We cover coconut water's pros and cons in our guide to [coconut water for a hangover](/never-hungover/coconut-water-for-hangover).

### 3. Honey-Banana Oatmeal with a Pinch of Salt

**Best for:** when you want something warm and comforting but not heavy.

**Why it works:** oats are mild, filling, and release energy slowly, so you don't get a sugar spike and crash. Cooking them in water or milk adds fluid. Banana brings potassium, and a drizzle of honey gives a quick bit of sugar while the oats do the slower work.

**Ingredients (serves 1):**

- 50 g (about half a cup) rolled oats
- 250 ml (about one cup) milk, water, or half and half
- 1 banana, sliced
- 1 teaspoon honey or maple syrup
- A pinch of salt
- Optional toppings: a spoonful of Greek yogurt or peanut butter for protein, a sprinkle of cinnamon, a few berries

**How to make it:**

1. Put the oats, liquid, and salt in a small pan over medium heat.
2. Stir every minute or so for about 5 minutes, until thick and creamy. (In a microwave: 2 to 3 minutes in a large bowl, stirring halfway.)
3. Stir in half the banana slices so they melt in.
4. Top with the rest of the banana, the honey, and a spoonful of yogurt or peanut butter.

**Make it savory:** if sweet food turns your stomach, cook the oats in broth, then top with a soft-boiled egg, a little soy sauce, and sliced green onion. Savory oatmeal is a great salty, protein-rich option and surprisingly good.

### 4. Egg and Potato Breakfast Burrito

**Best for:** the "I need something substantial" hangover, once your stomach has settled.

**Why it works:** this is the healthier version of the greasy breakfast you're craving. Potatoes are a good source of potassium and easy carbs, eggs bring protein, and the tortilla makes it easy to eat. It feels indulgent but isn't swimming in oil.

**Ingredients (serves 1):**

- 1 medium potato, diced small (or a handful of leftover cooked potatoes)
- 2 eggs
- 1 large flour tortilla
- A small handful of grated cheese
- 1 teaspoon oil
- Salt and pepper
- Optional: a spoonful of black beans, mild salsa, a few slices of avocado

**How to make it:**

1. Microwave the diced potato in a covered bowl for 3 to 4 minutes until just soft. This saves a lot of frying time.
2. Heat the oil in a pan over medium heat and add the potato with a pinch of salt. Cook for 5 minutes, turning, until lightly golden.
3. Push the potatoes to one side, crack in the eggs, and scramble them gently.
4. Warm the tortilla in a dry pan or the microwave for 15 seconds.
5. Fill it with the potatoes, eggs, cheese, and any extras. Fold in the sides and roll it up.

**Go easy on:** hot sauce and spicy salsa. Spicy food can aggravate a stomach that's already irritated by alcohol, and it's a common heartburn trigger. If you tend to get acid after drinking, our guide to [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) has more on what to avoid.

### 5. Gentle Rice Porridge (Congee) or Broth with Toast

**Best for:** nausea, a sensitive stomach, or when nothing else appeals.

**Why it works:** rice porridge is a breakfast staple across much of Asia and a traditional food for people who feel unwell. It's very soft, mostly water, lightly salted, and about as gentle on the stomach as food gets. You get fluid, salt, and easy carbs in one bowl. A simple broth with a slice of toast does the same job if you don't have time to make porridge.

**Ingredients (serves 1 to 2):**

- 1 cup cooked rice (leftover rice is perfect)
- 2 to 3 cups chicken, vegetable, or miso broth
- A thin slice of fresh ginger
- Salt or a splash of soy sauce to taste
- Optional: a soft-boiled egg, shredded cooked chicken, sliced green onion

**How to make it:**

1. Put the cooked rice, broth, and ginger slice in a pan and bring to a simmer.
2. Cook for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring now and then and mashing the rice against the side of the pan, until it breaks down into a thick, soupy porridge. Add more broth or water if it gets too thick.
3. Remove the ginger, season with salt or soy sauce, and top with an egg or chicken if you can manage it.
4. Eat it slowly, in small spoonfuls.

**The 2-minute version:** heat a mug of broth, add a pinch of salt, and have it with a slice of dry toast. That's a perfectly good starting point when your stomach is fragile. For more ideas, see our guide to the [best soups for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-soups-for-hangover).

## What to Eat for a Hangover Breakfast If You Feel Sick

If you're nauseous, the order you do things matters more than the recipe.

1. **Fluid first, in small sips.** A few mouthfuls of water or an electrolyte drink every few minutes is easier to keep down than a whole glass at once.
2. **Then something plain and dry.** Dry toast, crackers, or a few bites of banana. Give it 30 to 60 minutes.
3. **Then something soft and warm.** Broth, rice porridge, or plain oatmeal.
4. **Then protein.** A soft-boiled or scrambled egg, or a little yogurt, once the earlier steps have stayed down.

Avoid forcing a big meal on a churning stomach. It tends to come back up, and losing fluid by vomiting sets you back further. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) has more ways to settle your stomach. If you can't keep fluids down for several hours, that's a reason to get medical advice rather than waiting it out.

## Is Greasy Food Good for a Hangover?

The full fry-up is the most famous hangover breakfast, so it deserves a straight answer: **there is no good evidence that greasy food speeds up hangover recovery.**

The idea probably comes from something that is true. Eating fat and protein **before or while** you drink slows down how fast alcohol is absorbed from your stomach into your blood. That can make a night of drinking a bit gentler. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) explains that part. But by the next morning, the alcohol has already been absorbed. Fat at breakfast can't undo that.

What a greasy breakfast does give you is comfort, salt, calories, and the feeling of being full, and those aren't nothing. The downsides are that heavy, fatty food digests slowly, can make nausea worse, and is a common trigger for heartburn and loose stools, which alcohol already encourages.

**The middle ground:** if you really want the full breakfast, keep it moderate. Choose eggs (scrambled or poached rather than deep-fried), a slice of toast, grilled tomatoes or mushrooms, and maybe one rasher of bacon or one sausage rather than the full plate. Have a big glass of water with it.

## Fast Food Hangover Breakfast: The Least-Bad Options

Sometimes you're not cooking. If you're at a drive-through:

- **Pick an egg-based sandwich or wrap.** An egg muffin or egg-and-cheese bagel gives you protein, carbs, and salt in a reasonable portion.
- **Skip or share the hash brown.** It's mostly oil and adds little except heaviness.
- **Order water or orange juice, not a large soda.** A big sugary soda gives you a quick sugar rush and nothing else, and fizzy drinks can bloat an upset stomach.
- **Oatmeal or a fruit cup** is often on the menu and is a gentle choice if your stomach is shaky.
- **Go easy on the coffee size.** A regular coffee is fine for most people. An extra-large one on an empty, irritated stomach can make you jittery.

## Hangover Breakfast Ideas: What to Drink With It

What you drink with breakfast matters as much as what you eat.

- **Water:** the baseline. Start with a large glass before you eat and keep a bottle nearby all morning.
- **Electrolyte or oral rehydration drinks:** better than plain water if you drank a lot, sweated, or were sick. Our comparison of [Pedialyte vs Gatorade for hangovers](/never-hungover/pedialyte-vs-gatorade-hangover) looks at the differences.
- **Coconut water:** a pleasant source of fluid and potassium, though lower in sodium than a proper rehydration drink.
- **Orange juice:** gives you fluid, sugar, and vitamin C. Fine in moderation, but it's acidic, so skip it if you have heartburn.
- **Coffee or tea:** if you normally drink coffee, a usual-sized cup can ease a headache that is partly caffeine withdrawal. It won't sober you up or rehydrate you, so have water alongside it. If your heart is racing or your stomach is burning, skip it for now.
- **Ginger or peppermint tea:** soothing and hydrating, and ginger may help nausea.
- **More alcohol ("hair of the dog"):** don't. Another drink only delays the hangover by topping up your blood alcohol, and it adds to the total your liver has to deal with.

## Foods to Skip the Morning After

- **Very spicy food.** Can aggravate an irritated stomach and trigger heartburn.
- **Large greasy meals.** Slow to digest and can worsen nausea (see above).
- **Very sugary breakfasts on their own.** A pastry and a sugary drink give a short lift followed by a dip. If you want something sweet, pair it with protein.
- **Acidic foods if you have reflux.** Citrus juice, tomato-heavy dishes, and coffee can all make heartburn worse.
- **Raw eggs in "hangover cocktails."** They carry a small risk of salmonella and offer nothing a cooked egg doesn't.

## Popular "Hangover Foods": What the Evidence Says

You'll see plenty of claims about specific foods online. Here's an honest take on the most common ones.

- **Eggs:** contain cysteine, which the body uses to make glutathione. The chemistry is real, but there is no good evidence from human trials that eating eggs makes a hangover shorter or milder. They're still an excellent, gentle breakfast. If you're curious about the supplement form, see our guide to [L-cysteine for hangovers](/never-hungover/l-cysteine-for-hangover).
- **Bananas:** an easy source of carbs and potassium. Sensible, not magic.
- **Asparagus:** a lab study using cells found asparagus extracts affected enzymes involved in breaking down alcohol, which led to a lot of headlines. That's a long way from showing that eating asparagus helps a hangover in people.
- **Pickle juice:** salty, so it may help a little with lost sodium. Many people find it too harsh on a hungover stomach, and a proper electrolyte drink does the same job more pleasantly.
- **Honey:** a quick source of sugar, which can help with that weak, shaky feeling. Claims that its fructose speeds up alcohol clearance haven't been backed up by good human evidence.
- **Toast:** plain, bland, and easy to keep down. Not exciting, but a reliable first step.

## Timing: When to Eat Your Hangover Breakfast

- **Drink first.** Have a glass of water or electrolyte drink as soon as you wake.
- **Eat within a couple of hours if you can.** Most people feel noticeably steadier once they've eaten. If you're not hungry, a few bites of toast or half a banana is enough to start.
- **Eat before any painkiller.** If you need one for a headache, taking it with food is easier on your stomach. Ibuprofen, naproxen, and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated, so food matters even more with those. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver, so it's best to wait until the alcohol has cleared, stick to a single standard dose, and avoid it if you drink heavily on a regular basis. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Have a second small meal later.** A light lunch a few hours later keeps your energy steady as your appetite returns.

## A Simple Hangover Morning Routine

Put together, a good morning looks like this:

1. **Wake up:** drink a large glass of water or an electrolyte drink.
2. **Within an hour:** start with something small and plain if your stomach is unsettled.
3. **Breakfast:** one of the five breakfasts above, eaten slowly.
4. **All morning:** keep sipping fluids. Pale yellow urine is a reasonable sign you're catching up.
5. **Rest:** a nap, a short walk in fresh air, or both. Sleep is a big part of recovery.
6. **Later:** a light lunch, and no more alcohol today.

## Where DHM Fits In

Breakfast helps you recover from a hangover. It doesn't do much to stop one from happening. Most of the real leverage is the night before: how much you drink, how fast, whether you eat beforehand, and whether you alternate with water. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers those basics.

Some people also take DHM (dihydromyricetin), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, before or while drinking. Animal studies suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and it's widely used as a hangover supplement, but human research is still limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone, and it is not a reason to drink more. If you want to try it, popular options include [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simple 1,000 mg DHM tablet, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and electrolytes. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. Either way, a good breakfast, water, and rest the next morning still matter.

## The Bottom Line

The best hangover breakfast is not a secret superfood. It's a simple plate that gives you fluid, salt, easy carbs, and gentle protein without upsetting your stomach. Soft scrambled eggs on toast is the reliable default. A banana-oat smoothie works when you can't face chewing. Oatmeal is the warm, gentle option. A potato-and-egg burrito satisfies the greasy craving without the grease. Rice porridge or broth is there for when your stomach is in revolt. Drink water first, eat slowly, and give your body the time it needs.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best breakfast for a hangover?**

A gentle, balanced plate works best: some protein (eggs or Greek yogurt), easy carbs (toast, oats, rice, or a banana), a little salt, and plenty of fluid. Soft scrambled eggs on toast with a banana and a glass of water or an electrolyte drink covers most of what your body is short on. No breakfast cures a hangover, but the right one can make the morning noticeably easier.

**Is greasy food good for a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that greasy food speeds up hangover recovery. Fat eaten before or during drinking slows how fast alcohol is absorbed, which is where the reputation comes from. The morning after, a heavy fry-up mostly makes you feel full and comforted, and for some people it worsens nausea or heartburn. If you want the comfort, keep the portion moderate and pair it with fluids.

**What should I eat for a hangover if I feel sick?**

Start with fluids in small sips, then plain, bland foods: dry toast, crackers, a banana, plain rice, or a simple broth. Ginger tea can help some people with nausea. Once those stay down for an hour or so, add a soft-cooked egg or some yogurt. If you can't keep fluids down for several hours or are vomiting repeatedly, get medical advice.

**Should I eat breakfast if I don't feel hungry after drinking?**

Yes, try to eat something small within a few hours of waking, even if it's just toast or a banana. Most people feel steadier once they eat, and food also makes it gentler to take a painkiller if you need one. You don't need a big meal. Small and simple is fine, and you can eat more later when your appetite comes back.

**Is coffee okay with a hangover breakfast?**

For regular coffee drinkers, a normal cup is usually fine and can ease a headache that is partly caffeine withdrawal. Coffee doesn't fix dehydration, so drink water alongside it, and skip it or keep it small if your stomach is irritated or your heart is racing. It is not a way to sober up.

**Are bananas good for a hangover?**

Bananas are a sensible choice. They are easy to digest, give you quick carbs, and contain potassium, a mineral you can lose some of when alcohol makes you urinate more. A banana won't cure a hangover on its own, but it's one of the easiest things to get down on a rough morning.

**Is a fast food breakfast sandwich good for a hangover?**

A fast food egg sandwich isn't the worst choice, because it gives you eggs, bread, and salt. The trouble is usually the size and grease of the full meal, plus a large sugary soda. If that's what's available, pick an egg-based sandwich, skip or share the hash brown, and get water or orange juice instead of soda.

**Does any breakfast actually cure a hangover?**

No. There is no good evidence that any food cures a hangover. Time is the only real cure. A good breakfast helps with the parts of a hangover that food can touch, such as low energy, an unsettled stomach, and mild dehydration, which is why many people feel better after eating.
